chapter: Brown's Band and Tom in Chicago
title: Dixieland combination versus older Black orchestras; competition
summary: Brown's band was a pioneer; Oliver and Armstrong's earlier bands were larger with violins; only Fisher's band competed.

story.theme_name: Remembering the early trumpeters and their styles
story.community_name: Remembering King Oliver: the man, the band, the decline

blocks.x: He deserved credit. Well, he was, in reality, a pioneer in the jazz field. And there was other colored bands that were up there. This was before Louis Armstrong came up there. This was before King Oliver and all those came up. King Oliver and the bands that King Oliver played, and Armstrong, when they first come up to New Orleans, it wasn't a Dick's land combination at all. They had violins, they had flutes, and they had about eight, ten, twelve men, so you understand. And they played regular music at all the other colored pieces. But the Dick's land combination, just five pieces, that's entirely different.
Yeah, Oliver, I think, got there about 1918, she saw it. And you say Papa Lane had mostly just the brass band. Mostly the brass band. And didn't do much dance work. No.

He'd take it to the small band. But I mean, you could see what... He'd play drums if he, maybe in the small combination. But I mean, I don't remember seeing, we didn't have no competition with these bands at all. In fact, the only bands that gave us competition, in respect, was Fisher's Band. And that band there, in the estimation of the dancers, and the people that I talked to that employed us, were second-raders in comparison to our band. And we played all the most exclusive affairs in New Orleans, up to the time I left them, in 1950.
